goal: Get comfortable with Rust ownership, borrowing and lifetimes so I can port a small Go CLI tool
interpretation: After about 4 hours of watching, the learner can reason about Rust ownership, borrowing and lifetimes with confidence, use Result and the ? operator idiomatically, and port their small Go CLI tool to Rust.
assumptions: The learner needs enough Rust syntax and tooling (cargo, structs, enums, match) to follow videos, but this is covered by mapping from Go rather than taught from scratch.
Traits are needed mainly as they relate to error handling, generics bounds and lifetimes, not as a full deep dive.
The ported CLI uses typical pieces: argument parsing (e.g. clap), file or stdin IO, and error propagation.
Videos in English; the learner prefers material aimed at experienced developers coming from Go, C, or C++.

sub_topics.title: Rust orientation for Go developers (cargo, structs, enums, match, Option)
sub_topics.why: Gives the minimum Rust vocabulary and tooling to follow ownership examples, mapped onto Go concepts they already know, without re-teaching variables or loops.

sub_topics.title: Ownership and moves (stack vs heap, move semantics, Copy vs Clone, Drop)
sub_topics.why: Go's GC hides ownership; this learner knows pointers and memory so can grasp move semantics quickly, but must internalize who owns and frees data.

sub_topics.title: Borrowing and references in depth (shared vs mutable borrows, borrow checker rules, common errors)
sub_topics.why: They want depth on the borrow checker; they need to understand aliasing XOR mutability and how to fix typical compiler errors, contrasted with Go pointers and slices.

sub_topics.title: Lifetimes (annotations, elision rules, structs holding references, 'static)
sub_topics.why: Lifetimes are the hardest part for newcomers and are needed for structs and functions that return references, such as parsed CLI config.

sub_topics.title: Traits and generics essentials (impl Trait, trait bounds, From, Display, Error trait)
sub_topics.why: Idiomatic error handling relies on traits such as std::error::Error, From and Display, which are unlike Go interfaces in key ways.

sub_topics.title: Error handling with Result and the ? operator (custom error types, thiserror, anyhow, From conversion)
sub_topics.why: Their Go CLI returns errors everywhere, so they need to translate if err != nil patterns into Result, ?, and custom or anyhow errors.

sub_topics.title: Build a Rust CLI project (clap, file IO, error propagation, ownership in practice)
sub_topics.why: A project-style walkthrough shows ownership, borrowing, lifetimes and Result working together in a tool like the one they are porting.

picks.title: Rust for Go Developers: The 6 Things You Actually Need to Learn
picks.reason: Maps Rust onto Go: ownership and borrowing, Result and Option, and compiler feedback. This suits a senior Go developer who needs orientation, not syntax basics. It is also the only candidate aimed at Go developers.
picks.confidence_note: Only metadata was assessed and there are no verified quotes or segment map. Depth is probably light, since the video is a six-topic overview.

picks.title: Understanding Ownership in Rust
picks.reason: A dedicated ownership video (moves, and likely Copy vs Clone and Drop) to build the move-semantics foundation before borrowing. It is the only candidate dedicated to ownership that is not flagged as a surface intro.
picks.confidence_note: The transcript was unavailable, so this is judged from the title and channel only. I would be more sure with a transcript showing stack/heap, moves, Clone and Drop at a non-beginner level.

picks.title: Understanding Rust – Or How to Stop Worrying & Love the Borrow-Checker • Steve Smith • YOW! 2024
picks.reason: A conference talk aimed at understanding the borrow checker, with the strongest borrowing relevance in the pool. It matches the learner's request for depth on the borrow checker. The pure_theory flag does not count against it here because the learner wants the concepts behind the checker.

picks.title: but what is 'a lifetime?
picks.reason: Explains what a lifetime is as a way of reasoning about references, a mental model that suits an experienced systems programmer. It comes before the annotation-focused videos.

picks.title: Rust Lifetimes explained Tutorial
picks.reason: Covers lifetime annotations, how the borrow checker validates references, and when explicit lifetime parameters are needed in function signatures and structs. This is the practical annotation side that follows the mental model.
picks.confidence_note: The transcript was not verified. It is unclear whether it covers elision rules and 'static in depth.

picks.title: Rust Generics, Traits & Lifetimes Explained — Book Chapter 10 Project
picks.reason: Works through generics, traits and lifetimes on a Rust Book Chapter 10 project, showing lifetimes in structs and function signatures alongside trait bounds. This sets up the trait knowledge that error handling needs.
picks.confidence_note: The transcript is poor and the video is based on the Rust Book, so it may be gentler than this learner needs. No segment map was available.

picks.title: Introduction to Generics and Traits | Advanced Rust Part 1
picks.reason: Introduces trait definitions and generic type parameters as Rust's alternative to inheritance. This gives the trait and bounds grounding that From, Display and the Error trait build on.
picks.confidence_note: The transcript was unavailable. It may not reach impl Trait, From or the Error trait specifically.

picks.title: Rust Error Handling: The ? Operator, thiserror & anyhow
picks.reason: Directly covers the ? operator, custom error types, From conversions, and thiserror vs anyhow (libraries vs applications). This maps onto the learner's Go habit of returning errors everywhere.
picks.confidence_note: The summary is detailed and matches the need, but there is no verified transcript or quote. Only an overview segment was listed.

picks.title: Build a Rust CLI Tool from Scratch (clap, serde, anyhow) – logscan
picks.reason: Builds a log-analysis CLI with clap, serde and anyhow, and works through a real borrow-checker error (E0515) during development. This shows ownership, borrowing and error propagation in a project close to the learner's port.
picks.confidence_note: The transcript is poor, and the segment map (00:12-04:19) does not match the 13-minute duration. Depth is unverified.

warnings: Every candidate was assessed from metadata only: no transcripts were available and there are no verified quotes. All evidence_quote_ids are empty and confidences are moderate to low. Skim each video's opening minutes before committing.

Total viewing time is about 191 minutes of the 240-minute budget (about 80%). The remaining 49 minutes were left unused because the remaining candidates were redundant, beginner-level, flagged, or had no usable transcript.
Coverage of Drop, Copy vs Clone and 'static is unverified. The ownership video and the lifetimes videos were chosen from titles and summaries.
No candidate is explicitly for Go developers beyond the 7.5-minute orientation. You will need to map Go's error returns and pointers to Result and references yourself when porting.
The CLI video covers clap, serde and anyhow with the file/log processing the learner needs. It is short (13 minutes), so expect to consult the clap docs for your own tool's argument layout.
Some upload dates are in the future relative to other metadata (e.g. 2026), so I assumed these are metadata errors and treated the material as current.
The plan has 9 picks from 9 different creators, so expect a different codebase and style for each video. This was accepted because no single creator covered all sub-topics.
